title: Why is `withColumn` in a loop an anti-pattern — each call re-analyzes the entire plan (driver-side overhead grows O(n²)), stacking projections that the optimizer must later merge — and what is the fix (use `select` with all column expressions at once, or `withColumns` in Spark 3.3+)?
shortTitle: Why withColumn in a loop is an anti-pattern

s1_definition.profdef: Calling `withColumn` inside a loop is an anti-pattern because each call returns a new DataFrame whose logical plan wraps the previous one in another Project node, and Spark re-analyzes and re-resolves the growing plan on the driver each time. For n columns this produces a deeply nested plan and roughly O(n squared) driver-side analysis cost, which can make plan construction extremely slow even before any data is processed. The fix is to add all columns in a single `select` with every column expression at once, or to use `withColumns` (a map of name to expression) introduced in Spark 3.3.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine adding one new column to the National Bank's report by rewriting the entire report from scratch each time, then doing that again for the next column, and again — a hundred times. Each rewrite re-reads and re-checks everything that came before, so the hundredth addition re-processes ninety-nine layers. Instead, you list all hundred columns once and build the report in a single pass. The loop rebuilds the whole plan repeatedly; the single select builds it once.
s1_definition.oneliner: withColumn in a loop re-analyzes a deepening plan each iteration (O(n squared) on the driver); add all columns at once with a single select or withColumns.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Calling `withColumn` inside a loop is an anti-pattern because each call returns a new DataFrame whose logical plan wraps the previous one in another Project node, and Spark re-analyzes and re-resolves the growing plan on the driver each time. For n columns this produces a deeply nested plan and roughly O(n squared) driver-side analysis cost, which can make plan construction extremely slow even before any data is processed. The fix is to add all columns in a single `select` with every column expression at once, or to use `withColumns` (a map of name to expression) introduced in Spark 3.3.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine adding one new column to the National Bank's report by rewriting the entire report from scratch each time, then doing that again for the next column, and again — a hundred times. Each rewrite re-reads and re-checks everything that came before, so the hundredth addition re-processes ninety-nine layers. Instead, you list all hundred columns once and build the report in a single pass. The loop rebuilds the whole plan repeatedly; the single select builds it once.

**One line to remember:** withColumn in a loop re-analyzes a deepening plan each iteration (O(n squared) on the driver); add all columns at once with a single select or withColumns.

sections.s2_technical:
Spark DataFrames are immutable and lazy. Each transformation returns a new DataFrame with a new logical plan that references the previous plan. `withColumn` adds exactly one column and produces a new plan node, a Project, wrapping the prior plan. Call it in a loop a hundred times and you get a hundred nested Project nodes.

The cost is on the driver, during analysis, not during execution. Every time you call `withColumn`, Spark analyzes and resolves the resulting plan — checking column names, types, and references — over the entire nested structure built so far. As the plan grows, each additional call must walk a larger tree, so the total analysis work grows quadratically, roughly O(n squared) for n columns. For large n this can take minutes or even hit stack-overflow-like deep recursion, all before a single row is read. The Catalyst optimizer will later collapse the stacked Projects into one, but it still has to build and analyze the deep plan first, which is the waste.

The fix is to express all the new columns in one step. With a single `select` you list every existing column plus every new expression at once: `df.select("*", expr1.alias("a"), expr2.alias("b"), ...)`, producing one Project node and one analysis pass. From Spark 3.3 there is `withColumns`, which takes a dictionary of column name to expression and adds them all in a single call: `df.withColumns({"a": expr1, "b": expr2})`. Both approaches build the plan once instead of n times.

A senior nuance: a handful of withColumn calls is perfectly fine and readable — the anti-pattern specifically bites when you loop over many columns, for example dynamically casting or deriving dozens of fields. In that case accumulate the expressions in a list or dict and apply them in one select or withColumns. This is a plan-construction optimization; it does not change results, only how fast Spark builds and analyzes the query.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank ingests a wide transactions file where fifty string columns must be cast to proper types. A developer looped `withColumn` fifty times, and the job spent minutes just building the plan on the driver before reading any data. This is exactly the O(n squared) analysis anti-pattern.

Problem 2 — The fix is to collect the cast expressions and apply them in one select, so the plan is built once. This is exactly the single-select remedy.

Problem 3 — On Spark 3.3 the same can be done cleanly with withColumns. This demonstrates the modern fix.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`WithColumnDemo`) that derives several columns for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) both the slow looping way and the fast single-select and withColumns way, and times the plan construction.

sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/withcolumn_demo.py
# Contrasts looping withColumn vs single select/withColumns for the bank.
import logging, time
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from derive.column_builder import ColumnBuilder

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("WithColumnDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return SparkSession.builder.appName("WithColumnDemo").getOrCreate()

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    df = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", 50000.0), ("CUR3001", 25000.0)], ["account_id", "amount"])
    builder = ColumnBuilder(n=50)

    t0 = time.time()
    slow = builder.loop_withcolumn(df)       # ANTI-PATTERN: 50 nested Projects
    log.warning("Loop withColumn plan built in %.3fs (O(n^2) analysis)",
                time.time() - t0)

    t1 = time.time()
    fast = builder.single_select(df)         # FIX: one Project, one analysis
    log.info("Single select plan built in %.3fs", time.time() - t1)

    t2 = time.time()
    fast2 = builder.with_columns(df)         # FIX (Spark 3.3+): withColumns dict
    log.info("withColumns plan built in %.3fs", time.time() - t2)

    log.info("Results identical; showing single-select output:")
    fast.show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/derive/column_builder.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

class ColumnBuilder:
    """Builds N derived columns three ways to contrast plan cost."""
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.n = n

    def _exprs(self):
        # N derived columns: fee_i = amount * (0.001 * (i+1))
        return {f"fee_{i}": F.col("amount") * F.lit(0.001 * (i + 1))
                for i in range(self.n)}

    def loop_withcolumn(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        # ANTI-PATTERN: each iteration re-wraps and re-analyzes the plan
        for name, expr in self._exprs().items():
            df = df.withColumn(name, expr)
        return df

    def single_select(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        # FIX: all new columns in ONE select -> one Project node
        cols = [F.col(c) for c in df.columns]
        cols += [expr.alias(name) for name, expr in self._exprs().items()]
        return df.select(*cols)

    def with_columns(self, df: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
        # FIX (Spark 3.3+): add all columns in a single call
        return df.withColumns(self._exprs())
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts with an amount; fifty derived fee columns to add.

Step 1: `loop_withcolumn` calls `withColumn` fifty times. The first call wraps the base plan in one Project; the second wraps that in another; by the fiftieth there are fifty nested Projects. Each call triggers analysis over the whole nested plan, so total analysis cost grows quadratically — this is the anti-pattern, and the log shows it is the slowest to build.

Step 2: `single_select` builds a list of all existing columns plus all fifty fee expressions and calls `select` once, producing a single Project and one analysis pass. The plan builds far faster.

Step 3: `with_columns` passes a dictionary of all fifty name-to-expression pairs in one `withColumns` call, also producing a single addition and one analysis pass.

Step 4: All three produce identical results because the operation is the same; only plan construction speed differs. The single-select output shows the two accounts with their fee columns.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Calling withColumn inside a loop is an anti-pattern because of how Spark builds plans. DataFrames are immutable and lazy, so each withColumn returns a new DataFrame whose logical plan wraps the previous one in another Project node. If I loop and call it fifty times, I get fifty nested Project nodes, and critically, every call makes Spark analyze and resolve the entire growing plan on the driver — checking names, types, and references over a bigger and bigger tree each time. That makes the total analysis cost grow roughly quadratically, O of n squared, for n columns, so with many columns the job can spend minutes just constructing the plan before it reads a single row. The optimizer does eventually collapse those stacked Projects into one, but it still had to build and analyze the deep plan first, which is the waste.

The fix is to add all the columns in a single step so the plan is built once. I accumulate every new column expression and apply them with one select that lists all existing columns plus all the new expressions, which produces a single Project and one analysis pass. Or, on Spark 3.3 and later, I use withColumns, which takes a dictionary of column name to expression and adds them all in one call. Both build the plan once instead of n times, and importantly neither changes the result — this is purely a plan-construction optimization.

At the National Bank of India this bit us on a wide ingestion job that cast fifty string columns to proper types with a withColumn loop, and the driver spent minutes building the plan before any data moved. I collected the fifty cast expressions into a list and applied them in a single select, and the plan construction dropped to a fraction of a second. The nuance I always add is that a handful of withColumn calls is perfectly fine and readable; the anti-pattern only bites when you loop over many columns, so whenever I am deriving dozens of fields dynamically I accumulate the expressions and apply them once with select or withColumns.
